slides.0.title: Diploma tasting and essays
slides.0.subtitle: Blind-tasting clues and an MW essay frame
slides.1.title: Blind-tasting clues (reasoning aids)
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Chenin Blanc
slides.1.highlights.0.content: High acidity, honeyed apple and waxy texture; dryland old vines add concentration and minerality; oak adds texture. Against the Loire, South Africa usually shows riper fruit and a little more alcohol
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Pinotage and the Cape Blend
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Deep colour, red and black fruit, often smoke and spice; a Cape Blend with Pinotage has more personality than a straight Bordeaux blend
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Sauvignon Blanc
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Durbanville leans to grapefruit and gooseberry (between Sancerre and Marlborough); Elim to flint, smoke and saline minerality
slides.1.content: These are reasoning clues, not guaranteed answers: eliminate first, then narrow with climate, variety and alcohol.
slides.2.title: An MW essay frame
slides.2.highlights.0.title: A five-part structure
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Unpack the question → climate and geography → viticulture and varieties → winemaking and style → market and conclusion; each part needs at least one concrete region or rule as evidence
slides.2.highlights.1.title: A sample question
slides.2.highlights.1.content: "Discuss how the Benguela Current and altitude shape quality wine in the Cape." Contrast the three Hemel-en-Aarde wards, Elgin, Elim and the Swartland
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Mistakes to avoid
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Treating forecasts as results (such as the 2018 crop loss), treating trade jargon as legal standards (Reserve), or quoting area figures with no year
slides.2.content: Always attach a year and source to numbers; if unsure, prefer "about" and a range.
slides.3.title: Short-answer practice: question and marking points
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Question 1
slides.3.highlights.0.content: “Explain how Swartland’s climate, soils and viticulture affect the style and value of its Chenin Blanc.” (about 250 words)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Marking points for question 1
slides.3.highlights.1.content: ① hot, dry, low rainfall (about 200–500 mm), Atlantic cooling at night; ② Malmesbury shale and granite; ③ dry-farmed old bush vines → low yield, concentration, retained acidity; ④ winemaking: whole bunch, wild yeast, old barrels → texture; ⑤ value: from bulk raw material to premium single sites, the OVP seal; ⑥ limits: high cost of low yields, continuing loss of old vines
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Question 2
slides.3.highlights.2.content: “Assess whether the transformation of the South African wine industry since the 1990s has been successful.” (about 350 words)
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Marking points for question 2
slides.3.highlights.3.content: ① successes: quotas abolished (1992), KWV privatised (1997), the share of the crop made into consumer wine rising from under 30% to over 70%, the Swartland new wave and international acclaim; ② shortfalls: about 60% of export volume is bulk, low grape prices, shrinking vineyard area, leafroll, the 2020–2021 sales bans; ③ social: the legacy of the dop system and the 2007 transformation charter; ④ conclusion: the quality transformation has succeeded, the economic and social ones are unfinished
slides.3.content: Assessment questions need a verdict by dimension: score quality, economics and society separately.
Which should you NOT do in an essay?
A. Attach a year and source to figures
B. Treat a forecast as a final result
C. Use concrete regions as evidence
A forecast is not a result.
In a blind tasting, a white with high acidity, honeyed apple and waxy texture is most likely?
Chenin Blanc; still narrow it with climate and alcohol.
How may "Reserve" be used in an essay?
A. As a legal quality standard
B. As an unregulated trade term
